analysis.title: Watch Taiwan Not Treasuries To Time Top In Stocks
key_insights: Yield levels alone are the wrong question for timing an equity top. What matters is what is driving yields and stocks. Yields have not risen in a way that is seriously hostile to the equity rally, and the higher-than-expected CPI print on Oct 14 is unlikely on its own to reverse the AI trade.

Stocks are only modestly overbought relative to Treasuries, and slightly less so after the Treasury rally over the prior 24 hours. This view shows no intense pressure to rebalance from equities to bonds.
Higher yields have already hurt stocks through lower forward P/E multiples, but strong forward revenue and margin growth have more than offset it, so the S&P 500 is holding up.

On Damodaran's measure, the implied equity risk premium is 3.67%. It uses earnings expectations out to five years and the index's internal rate of return in excess of the Treasury yield. Adding the Treasury yield gives an expected S&P return of almost 9%, which has climbed in recent months even as yields rose.

Expected earnings are rising at an unprecedented rate. The sum of the next three years of projected S&P earnings is growing at about a 40% annual pace, the fastest in the available data. This rise dominates the drop in present value from a higher discount rate.

Since the Iran war, or since Kevin Warsh's speech at Jackson Hole, almost all of the rise in nominal yields has come from real yields, including the recent pullback to about 5.10%. This points to stronger real growth expectations, not fiscal risk. Fiscal risk would show up in higher breakevens.
The next leg depends on earnings expectations staying elevated. If they turn, stocks look much more vulnerable with yields still above 5%.

Analysts' capex expectations are a lagging indicator, and a single headline about a large tech firm pulling back is not knowable ahead of time. South Korean and Taiwanese exports are the proposed early signal of a pervasive capex problem.

South Korea and Taiwan are small, highly cyclical economies and major producers of AI chips. Their exports rose early this year before earnings expectations increased, and they currently show little sign that the investment cycle is about to turn down.

Both export series are monthly and released at the start of each month. South Korea also publishes a first-10-days estimate around the 21st. Chip exports are expected to detect a capex pullback with about a 3-6 month lead.

When chip exports fall, yields should also decline, since exports lead nominal GDP and the rise in real growth expectations has driven yields higher. The sequencing is uncertain: a capex shock could lower stocks and yields together, or hit earnings expectations first and leave stocks exposed to yields above 5%.

sector_views.rationale: The AI investment cycle shows no imminent downturn in Korean and Taiwanese chip exports, and earnings expectations are still rising. The author flags chip exports as the leading indicator for when to turn cautious.

earnings_insights: Sum of the next three years of projected S&P 500 earnings is rising at about a 40% annual pace, the fastest in the available data (projected figure, not a reported print).
Forward revenue and margin growth are described as very strong and are offsetting the drag on forward P/E multiples from higher yields.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Described as unlikely on its own to reverse the AI trade. The report gives no numeric value.
Uses five-year earnings expectations. Adding the Treasury yield gives an expected S&P 500 return of almost 9%, which supports stocks despite higher yields.

Almost all of the rise since the Iran war or the Warsh Jackson Hole speech came from real yields, which implies stronger real growth expectations. Stocks look more vulnerable at yields above 5% if earnings expectations turn.
Equals the implied ERP plus the Treasury yield. It has risen in recent months, which explains why stocks rallied as yields rose.
The fastest rise in the available data. It outweighs the discount-rate effect of higher yields.

risk_factors: A turn in earnings expectations would leave stocks vulnerable with yields still above 5%.
A pervasive AI capex slowdown, which South Korean and Taiwanese chip exports should detect with a 3-6 month lead.
A capex shock could hit stocks and yields together, or hit earnings expectations first and leave stocks exposed to yields above 5%.
A rise in yields driven by fiscal risk, shown by higher breakevens, would be hostile to stocks. The author says this is not what is happening now.
vol_and_positioning: Stocks are modestly overbought relative to Treasuries, slightly less so after the Treasury rally over the prior 24 hours, so there is no intense pressure for a rebalancing from equities to bonds.
geopolitical: The Iran war is cited as a starting point for the rise in nominal yields, which was driven by real yields.
Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech is cited as another starting point for the rise in real yields.

tension_points.bull_case: Yields are rising on stronger real growth expectations. Expected S&P 500 returns are near 9% and three-year earnings expectations are rising about 40% a year, which outweighs the higher discount rate.
tension_points.bear_case: If earnings expectations turn, stocks look much more vulnerable with yields still above 5%. A capex shock could lower stocks and yields together.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A decline in South Korean and Taiwanese chip exports, which would signal a pervasive capex pullback with a 3-6 month lead.
